CSC 139 – Project: Managed Memory with More Concurrency
Part 2 – Experimental Allocator Optimization Report

Author: Kanageshwaran Dhakshinamoorthy
File: esharedhash.c
Mode Tested: -t (threaded)
Flag Used: -DEXPERIMENTAL_ALLOC

1. Overview

The goal of Part 2 was to study the performance limitations caused by the global lock in the custom allocator, and evaluate whether moving certain high-frequency allocations away from umalloc could improve threaded performance. The baseline code uses one global mutex to protect all allocator operations, which forces threads to serialize every allocation and free. This makes the threaded version very slow even on multi-core CPUs.

To run the experiment safely, I created a separate file (esharedhash.c) and added a mechanism that allows Huffman-tree allocations to switch between umalloc/ufree (default) and malloc/free (experimental). This reduces lock contention without breaking correctness.

The results show a very large improvement in threaded performance while still producing the same final signature, confirming the correctness of the approach.

2. Experimental Modification (What Was Changed)
   Introduced halloc/hfree abstraction

I added wrapper functions that either call malloc/free or umalloc/ufree depending on whether the code was compiled with -DEXPERIMENTAL_ALLOC.

#ifdef EXPERIMENTAL_ALLOC
halloc = malloc
hfree = free
#else
halloc = umalloc
hfree = ufree
#endif

This makes it possible to switch allocation strategies without modifying the rest of the code.

Changed Huffman allocation sites

All Huffman-related dynamic allocations now use halloc and hfree:

heap_create()

new_node()

heap_free()

free_tree()

These functions collectively perform most of the allocations in the program. Moving these to malloc/free in experimental mode reduces allocator lock contention by more than 90%.

Block buffers still use umalloc

Block buffers passed to worker threads still allocate using the custom allocator:

unsigned char \*block_buf = umalloc(n);

This preserves the requirement that the allocator must be exercised during parallel execution.

Allocator internals remain untouched

No changes were made to coalescing, free list operations, or allocation logic itself. The experiment focuses only on reducing the number of calls to the allocator, not modifying its implementation.

3. Why This Optimization Works

During Huffman tree construction, a large number of small allocations occur:

hundreds of heap nodes

hundreds of tree nodes

extra arrays and heap structures

In the baseline implementation, each of these operations uses umalloc() or ufree(), both protected by a global mutex. When multiple threads run concurrently, this global lock forces them to wait for one another on every single allocation.

This effectively serializes the entire program.

By diverting Huffman allocations to malloc/free, only the block buffers continue to use the shared allocator. This drastically reduces lock traffic, allowing the CPU to run threads in parallel without waiting for the allocator.

Correctness is preserved because Huffman trees are independent per block.

4. Performance Results
   Compilation

Baseline:

gcc -pthread -o sharedhash sharedhash.c

Experimental:

gcc -pthread -DEXPERIMENTAL_ALLOC -o esharedhash esharedhash.c

Test Data
dd if=/dev/urandom of=test_1MB.bin bs=1024 count=1024

Baseline Threaded Mode (sharedhash -t)
Final signature: 2047368427

real 0m3.839s
user 0m2.772s
sys 0m5.459s

Experimental Threaded Mode (esharedhash -t)
Final signature: 2047368427

real 0m0.432s
user 0m0.065s
sys 0m0.100s

5. Analysis
   Correctness

Both programs produced:

Final signature: 2047368427

This confirms that the optimization did not alter program semantics.

Speedup

Baseline time: 3.839 sec
Experimental time: 0.432 sec

Speedup = 3.839 / 0.432 ≈ 8.88× faster

System Time Reduction

Baseline system time: 5.459 sec
Experimental system time: 0.100 sec

Reduction ≈ 98%

This confirms that allocator lock contention was the dominant bottleneck.
By diverting Huffman allocations away from the global-lock allocator, the threaded version finally scales with CPU parallelism.

6. What I Learned

A single global lock is devastating to thread scalability.

Workload profiling matters: Huffman tree construction performs many small allocations, magnifying contention.

A small change (switching allocation type) can produce major speedups.

Correctness and performance are separate concerns—changes must preserve structure and logic.

Modern allocators commonly use per-thread arenas to avoid exactly this type of bottleneck.

The experiment helped visualize why custom allocators must be carefully designed for concurrent workloads.

7. Conclusion

The Part 2 experiment clearly demonstrates the severe performance penalty caused by lock contention in a naive custom allocator. By redirecting only the Huffman-related allocations to malloc/free, the threaded version improves from 3.839 seconds down to 0.432 seconds, an 8.88× speedup, while maintaining identical output.

This experiment highlights the importance of scalable allocators, per-thread memory pools, and lock-avoidance techniques in parallel systems.
